name: Zsh
summary: An interactive shell that parses commands into compact wordcode, executes pipelines and shell functions with job-control state, and extends its builtin surface through dynamically loadable modules and autoloading.

features.name: Wordcode parse and execution pipeline
features.description: The fixed source parses shell input into an internal wordcode program and executes it through execode, execpline, and related functions. The Zsh manual documents shell grammar, lists, pipelines, functions, and substitutions at the language boundary.
benefits: A compact intermediate program separates parsing from execution
The same execution machinery can run top-level commands, functions, and substitutions
costs: Wordcode and execution contexts add implementation-specific state
Shell grammar and expansion semantics remain highly interdependent

features.name: Job control and signal coordination
features.description: Zsh's execution code creates and waits for pipelines while job tables and signal handling track foreground, background, stopped, and completed processes. The official manual documents job control and process handling as shell behavior.
benefits: Composes Unix pipelines with interactive foreground and background control
Centralizes signal-driven process status in shell job state
costs: Signal timing and terminal process groups are OS-dependent
Nested execution and asynchronous jobs complicate cleanup and status propagation

features.name: Dynamic module and autoload boundary
features.description: Zsh maintains module tables and autoloadable definitions for builtins, conditions, parameters, and math functions. The manual documents dynamic modules and autoloading as extension mechanisms that add shell features on demand.
benefits: Keeps optional functionality outside the always-loaded core
Allows features to be installed and resolved through stable shell names
costs: Feature availability depends on module paths and load-time state
Module ABI and autoload failures cross the shell language boundary

mathematical_views.question: How does textual shell grammar become wordcode and then process, builtin, or function effects?
assumptions: Parsing produces a finite wordcode program with control-flow and command boundaries
Execution interprets wordcode under shell and job contexts
The view abstracts lexical details, signals, and platform-specific process calls

mathematical_views.model: Shell extension and job resource graph
mathematical_views.question: How do modules, autoloaded functions, shell contexts, pipelines, and job records connect?
assumptions: Modules and autoload definitions are extension resources, while jobs and process groups are execution resources
Edges represent feature resolution, command execution, process creation, or status propagation
The graph does not claim that every module or autoload path is enabled in every installation

costs: Intermediate state increases semantic and debugging complexity
Signals and process groups complicate lifecycle handling

benefits: Optional features can be loaded on demand
costs: Runtime availability and module compatibility become operational concerns
